terms.comment: Levi and Bini’s word for the Italian baccalà, salt cod (p. 8); for the hake they have another, merula (p. 42). It is not in Lewis & Short, Traupman or Morgan–Owens. In zoology the name is the hake’s: Linnaeus’s Gadus merluccius, now the genus Merluccius. For the fish itself the lexicon has the classical asellus (see cod).

phrases.english: cod preserved in salt and dried

merlucius.against: Levi and Bini print merlucius, ii without marks, and the word is not in Lewis & Short
merlucius.html: The long vowel is that of lūcius, the pike (Aus. Mos. 123, Lewis & Short), if the name is “sea pike”, mare with lūcius. That is one of two derivations given for the fish’s name, the other being from merula, and the ETYFish Project calls the etymology uncertain; so the length is probable, not established. No source marks the other vowels, and they are written short.

sources: Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 8, s.v. baccalà; p. 42, s.v. nasello.
Christopher Scharpf, The ETYFish Project: Family Merlucciidae (revised 14 November 2025).
